newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: FOCUS-NZ dlr climbs on Birch confidence in economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-NZ dlr climbs on Birch confidence in economy.

text.p: New Zealand's dollar surged higher on Wednesday after Finance Minister Bill Birch repeated a message he has taken round the world this week that the economy is poised for steady recovery and the currency is fairly valued.
Birch, speaking in Hong Kong after an investment tour that has already taken him to New York and London, said he thought export growth in 1996 suggested the dollar was not overvalued.

Dealers said his comments coincided with a squeeze on short positions in the New Zealand currency, adding that its sustained rally against both the yen and the U.S. dollar spread into short-term bank bills where interest rates eased around eight basis points.

Immediately after Birch spoke at around 0030 GMT, in a live interview with Reuters Financial Television, the dollar rose to about US$0.6925/32 from around 0.6900 and remained around that level for several hours.

Birch said he recognised that some exporters had been under pressure from low commodity prices, but argued this had been the main reason they had felt a squeeze in recent months rather than as a result of steady strengthening of their dollar.
"What I think one should recognise is that, even during this period, say right through calendar '96, our export volumes have steadily moved up.
"We have seen a 10 percent growth of export volumes across the export sector. That is not an indication of an overvalued exchange rate," he added.

While this view is less than universally-shared among exporters and financial market economists, Birch's comments on the general picture for the economy sounded a chord with new forecasts from the National Bank of New Zealand (NBNZ).

In a report headlined "The tide has turned", NBNZ economist Adrian Orr said the bank expects New Zealand to start moving out of its latest trough and able to support growth of about 3.0 percent per annum over the next three years.

While NBNZ saw question marks over a number of aspects of recovery, including concerns the growth would be largely funded by a sharp planned increase in government spending, it saw only modest swings in interest and currency rates going forward.
Birch also sought to play down market fears, shared by NBNZ among others, that the country's current account deficit will be a problem if it widens steadily as most economists have forecast.
He said the government was confident it could control the deficit even though it continued to be over four percent of GDP and was set to rise through 1997/98.
"If you look behind those numbers... that's manageable, and there is no undue concern about the current account deficit," he said.

Currency and money market dealers said the rally seen in the Kiwi and in short-dated bank bills and bill futures reflected prevailing trading positions and tight monetary conditions just as much as the finance minister's comments.
"The market was short," said a chief dealer.
"A lot of people were expecting Kiwi to break lower -- it was very close to that 0.6915 resistance -- so it only took a little bit for the market to push through there and all the shorts to stop out.
Other dealers said Birch's comments, while the catalyst for the Kiwi's move, did not hold a lot of weight.
"You've got to see it in the context of who he's talking to," said the chief dealer.

"It's been generally acknowledged that the offshore investors have been taking a slightly more stand-off attitude with New Zealand over the last three months and I think he's just doing damage control."
